clue.text: A nation fell for her ...

blocks.note: surface reading: a whole country fell in love with some woman
setter's reading: her name begins with a European nation, and she is the heroine of Dante's Inferno who fell for her lover Paolo

explanation.surface: A woman so charming that an entire country lost its heart to her.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue: she fell for her love. FRANCESCA da Rimini fell for Paolo, and her name starts with FRANCE, the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesca da Rimini is the famous adulterous lover in Dante, whose name opens with a country.

clue.text: View before a brimming mug?

blocks.note: a brimming cup is filled to the top
mug is slang for a face

explanation.surface: A glimpse of a tankard filled to the brim.
explanation.walkthrough: Mug suggests a drinking vessel to go with brimming; here it is slang for the face.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait taken from straight in front, showing the whole of the face, is that kind of view.

clue.text: In my absence a member is seen in a cautious light

indicators.note: in the absence of something means it is not there, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
my, from the setter's point of view, is me

explanation.surface: When I am away, a colleague is viewed with suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: On a British traffic light amber comes between red and green and tells drivers to proceed with caution.
explanation.definitionFit: The orange-yellow signal warns drivers to slow down and prepare to stop.

clue.text: Man of rank paints silver, they say

indicators.note: they say points to how the words are pronounced rather than written

blocks.note: to paint is to colour, and argent is the heraldic word for silver

explanation.surface: Someone senior gives things a silvery coat, so people report.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, the heraldic phrase runs into the army title. ARGENT is silver in heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior non-commissioned infantry officer in the British Army, ranking above a sergeant.

clue.text: Fruit and nut, alas mixed

indicators.note: mixed means stirred together, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: two words taken together as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sad note about a bag of fruit and nut mix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit and nut' reads like the chocolate bar or a trail mix; only 'Fruit' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sultana is a seedless dried white grape, a familiar dried fruit.

clue.text: Charged a hundred spent on account

blocks.note: AC is the standard abbreviation for account
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
spent money has been used up

explanation.surface: Billed for a hundred pounds paid out on credit.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed after: the hundred-spent part sits below the account.
explanation.definitionFit: A person charged with a crime is formally accused of it.

clue.text: ... love rejected with irritation

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read from the other end

blocks.note: a sore is a source of irritation; sore can mean irritated

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a lover turned away with annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots join this to the clue at 1 across, so the two read as one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of desire, and his name stands for passionate love itself.

clue.text: Vain error corrected in Galileo's towering view

indicators.note: an error that is corrected gets rewritten, so the letters are put right in a new order

blocks.note: two words taken together as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Galileo's mistaken vanity was put right by what he saw from a height.
explanation.walkthrough: Towering refers to the Leaning Tower of Pisa, from which Galileo is said to have dropped weights; Pisa stands on this river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tuscan river flows through Pisa, so it is what one sees from the leaning tower.

clue.text: Newsprint when used for a quick run

indicators.note: something used is no longer fresh, so the word meaning fresh is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Old newspaper put to use for a quick print run.
explanation.walkthrough: Used is the opposite of new, so the first three letters go.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprint is a short burst of running at full speed.

clue.text: Do they help one to contemplate a double Scotch?

definitions.text: Do they help one to contemplate a double Scotch?

blocks.note: surface reading: drinking vessels for a large whisky
setter's reading: spectacles with two-part lenses help the wearer look at something, near or far

explanation.surface: Asking whether certain tumblers are good for pondering a large whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Glasses suggests tumblers for a dram; here they are spectacles, and double points to their split lenses.
explanation.definitionFit: These spectacles have lenses with two focal lengths, one for reading and one for distance.

clue.text: Title tag from "La Belle Helene"

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the quoted title, lying inside it

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A caption borrowed from Offenbach's operetta about Helen of Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: A label is a tag naming or describing something, much as a title heads a work.

clue.text: Leading voice in choral setting of Western "Bride Snatcher"

indicators.note: the leading letter is the one at the front of the word
a musical setting rearranges material, so these letters are put in a new order
in tells us the first part is placed inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written
the opening letter of voice

explanation.surface: A choir's lead singer performing in a musical version of a cowboy story about stealing a bride.
explanation.walkthrough: Young LOCHINVAR, in Scott's poem Marmion, comes out of the west and carries off his love from her wedding to another man.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's hero rode in from the west and abducted a woman at her own wedding feast.

clue.text: This one is associated with motor racing

definitions.text: This one is associated with motor racing

blocks.clueFragment: This one is associated with motor racing
blocks.note: surface reading: some car or driver linked to the track
setter's reading: the word that comes before One in the name of the top racing series

explanation.surface: Pointing out something connected with motor sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Formula One is the premier grand prix series, so the answer is the word that goes with one.
explanation.definitionFit: The top class of motor racing is named Formula One, after the rules governing its cars.

clue.text: It's mostly worn above the Tweed, or river with bridge over

definitions.text: It's mostly worn above the Tweed

indicators.note: a bridge goes over something, here spanning the other letters on either side

blocks.note: a span is a bridge or the arch of one
taken as written
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Something largely worn on top of tweed cloth, or a river with a crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Above the Tweed' means north of the river Tweed, the border between England and Scotland, not on top of tweed fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: The pouch hangs from a kilt's belt, and is chiefly a piece of Scottish Highland dress.

clue.text: Transport by air is cheap and flexible

indicators.note: something flexible can be bent into another shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: four words taken together as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An advert claiming flights are inexpensive and adaptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport by air' looks like one phrase about flying; only 'Transport' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A light horse-drawn carriage pulled by two horses, an old form of conveyance.

clue.text: One could swill Brian's tea

indicators.note: to swill is to slosh liquid about, so these letters are swirled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone happy to gulp down a mug of Brian's tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a teetotaller would drink tea rather than alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: A teetotaller refrains from alcohol, so tea is the sort of drink such a person would gulp.

clue.text: One Tory lad stirs up misplaced veneration

indicators.note: stirring things up throws them into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A young Conservative causes trouble by worshipping the wrong thing.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Worship of images or false gods, or excessive devotion, is reverence directed wrongly.

clue.text: It may need tissues - about 500 sheets costing roughly £500

indicators.note: roughly means not exactly, so the letters are not kept in their given order
about means going around, so the rearranged letters surround the paper

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
L for pound, from the Latin libra, and D for the Roman numeral 500
a ream of paper is 500 sheets

explanation.surface: A pack of paper tissues priced at a large sum, sounding like a stationery order.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy head cold with a running nose has the sufferer reaching for paper hankies.

clue.text: Part of the audience may hear the voice of the prophet

indicators.note: hearing a voice means the word counts by its sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: an oracle is a prophet, one through whom a god speaks

explanation.surface: Someone in a theatre crowd might hear a seer speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: Audience here means the organs of hearing rather than a crowd of listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: The auricle is the visible outer ear, a part of the hearing apparatus.

clue.text: Stuck like a politician in false ideal

indicators.note: false means not genuine, so the word is not in its true order
in places the first item inside the second

blocks.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A politician trapped by a mistaken principle.
explanation.definitionFit: Being impaled means being pierced and pinned on a spike, so held fast.

clue.text: Deal possibly set aside

blocks.note: first meaning: a leftover piece of timber, deal being pine or fir board
second meaning: cut off and put to one side

explanation.walkthrough: Deal looks like a business agreement; it is softwood timber, a scrap of which could be the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A remnant sliced from a larger piece of wood or cloth and left over is called this.

clue.text: Idle quiche seller?

blocks.note: surface reading: a lazy trader in savoury tarts
setter's reading: a flan seller, named like a French trade with the ending -eur, is also the word for a loafer

explanation.surface: A lazy shopkeeper who sells egg tarts.
explanation.walkthrough: A FLANEUR is a man-about-town who strolls idly; split as FLAN plus -EUR, the French ending for a trader, it reads as a flan merchant.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loan word names an idle stroller who saunters about watching city life.

clue.text: Skittish, like Shaw?

blocks.note: first meaning: frisky and frolicsome
second meaning, read cryptically: George Bernard Shaw was full of plays

explanation.walkthrough: Read as PLAY-FUL, the word describes a prolific dramatist such as Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means frisky and fun-loving, and split apart it means brimming with dramas.

clue.text: Wells's partner had a long way to travel

blocks.note: far means a long distance
to go is to travel

explanation.surface: Someone's partner faced a lengthy journey.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells Fargo was the American stagecoach and banking firm founded by Henry Wells and William Fargo.
explanation.definitionFit: William Fargo co-founded the express company with Henry Wells, so he was the partner.

clue.text: Coin disposed through channel laid down by the church

indicators.note: disposed means arranged, so these letters take a new order
something passing through a channel ends up inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a canal is an artificial channel

explanation.surface: Money thrown into a waterway along a route set by the church.
explanation.definitionFit: Canon law is the body of rules the church prescribes, so its decrees are canonical.

clue.text: Dicky traps a modest catch

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or shaky, so these letters are out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Dicky sets traps and lands a small haul.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a man's name; it is the slang adjective for unsound, as in a dicky heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fish of the herring family, proverbially the bait used to land a mackerel.

clue.text: Foreign currency used to square rent

blocks.note: a T-square is the draughtsman's ruler, and its shape is the letter T
the ore is a coin of Sweden, Denmark and Norway

explanation.surface: Overseas money spent to settle a landlord's charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent looks like the money paid to a landlord, but it is the past tense of rend, to tear apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are past tenses of verbs meaning ripped apart forcibly, as in a garment rent asunder.

clue.text: Clinical insight

blocks.note: surface reading: a doctor's sharp understanding of a case
setter's reading: literally a sight inside, a look into the body in a hospital

explanation.surface: A doctor's shrewd diagnostic perception.
explanation.definitionFit: The procedure passes a camera tube into the body so doctors can look inside an organ.
